# Withdrawals

One JSON file per advisory, named `<ADVISORY-ID>.json`. This directory is the
**only** source of `registry/v1/revocations.json`; that file is generated by
`node tools/build-revocations.mjs` and CI fails if it differs by one byte from a
fresh generation.

Revocation is the only mechanism in the Astra plugin design that helps *after* a
bad plugin is already on somebody's machine. Everything else — the attestation,
the digest pin, the TOFU identity — decides whether bytes may arrive. So the
thing to get right here is not the format; it is that the daemon has five places
it enforces this list and that a wrong `kind` or a mistyped digest silently
matches nothing.

## Writing one

```json
{
  "id": "ASTRA-2026-0001",
  "published": "2026-08-14",
  "severity": "critical",
  "action": "disable",
  "reason": "Version 1.2.0 exfiltrates the contents of the clipboard to a third-party host.",
  "advisory_url": "https://github.com/mihailinl/astra-registry/security/advisories/ASTRA-2026-0001",
  "entries": [
    { "kind": "digest", "value": "9f2c…64 lowercase hex…" },
    { "kind": "version_range", "value": "example-plugin",
      "versions": { "introduced": "1.2.0", "fixed": "1.2.1" } }
  ]
}
```

`node tools/build-revocations.mjs` refuses anything the daemon would not read,
and says which field and why.

## `kind`

| `kind` | `value` is | Catches |
|---|---|---|
| `digest` | sha256 of the whole `.astraplugin`, 64 lowercase hex | **Prefer this.** The bytes, whichever route they took — the store, `ImportPluginFile`, or a USB stick |
| `binary` | sha256 of a resolved `entry.command` file | A sideloaded source directory, which has no archive and therefore no bundle digest. This is the enforcement point people forget |
| `id` | a plugin id | Every version, forever. A blunt instrument |
| `id_version` | `<id>@<semver>` | One release, when its digest is not to hand |
| `version_range` | a plugin id, with `versions.introduced` (inclusive) and `versions.fixed` (exclusive) | The usual shape of a real advisory |
| `identity` | `github:owner/repo` or `origin:host` | A publisher, when the account itself is the problem |
| `publisher_key` | a signing `key_id` | Everything one index key signed, after that key is compromised |

An advisory may carry several entries; each becomes one entry in the deployed
document, and each carries the advisory's `id`, `severity`, `action`, `reason`
and URL, because the daemon shows exactly one of them — the first that matches.

### At least one entry has to be able to see a directory

`digest` is the natural first reach and it is the right first entry — but it is
the sha256 of an **archive**, and a sideloaded source directory does not have
one. `sideload_plugin` matches against an id, a version and the hashes of the
files it is about to execute, and nothing else; a digest-only advisory is
therefore fully in force and matches nothing on the one route that has nothing
else to key on. Copy `plugin.toml` and the binary into a folder, sideload, and
the withdrawal is gone.

So `build-revocations.mjs` **refuses** an advisory whose entries are all
`digest` (or all `digest`/`identity`/`publisher_key` — a directory has no signer
either). At least one of `binary`, `id`, `id_version` or `version_range` has to
be there. `version_range` is usually the honest one; `id` is the blunt one; and
`binary` is
`sha256(<the file `entry.command` resolves to inside the bundle>)`, which is
exactly what the daemon hashes at every sideload and every start.

## `action`

| `action` | The daemon |
|---|---|
| `block_install` | refuses new installs and updates; an installed copy keeps running |
| `disable` | refuses installs **and** stops, disables and refuses to start what is already there |
| `warn` | badges it and tells the user; changes nothing else |

`severity` is advisory only. Nothing the daemon does hangs on it, deliberately:
if behaviour keyed off severity, anyone who reached the signing key could
downgrade a withdrawal to "low" instead of removing it.

An action the daemon does not recognise is read as `disable`. That is the safe
direction — a newer registry inventing a spelling and an older daemon reading it
as "do nothing" would be a withdrawal that silently did not happen — but it
means a typo here is a *stronger* action than intended, not a weaker one.

## Undoing one

Delete the advisory file and republish. The serial goes up (it is the commit
count of this directory), and the daemon replaces its whole set on a strictly
greater serial. On a lower or equal serial it may only *add*, which is what
stops a replayed old document from removing a withdrawal — and is why deleting
the file is the only way to undo one.

## Built-in sidecars are out of scope

`astra-vox` and `astra-stt` ship with the daemon. They have no bundle, no digest
and no trust record, and the daemon exempts them from all five enforcement
points by design: the remedy for a bad sidecar is an Astra release, and the
registry has no authority to switch off somebody's microphone. An entry naming
one of them is inert.
